INTRODUCTIONM
This lesson introduces the principles and concepts of aircraft temperature, and fuel flow indicating systems instruments.
Aircraft Instrumentation provides the technician and flight crew with an indication of how the vital aircraft systems are performing.
Flight crews need to continuously monitor the outside air, the engine exhaust and the engine oil temperatures to ensure they remain in normal operating ranges.

1. Temperature and Fuel Flowmeter Instruments
LESSON MENU
TEMPERATURE AND FUEL FLOW INSTRUMENTSMENTS
DISCUSSION
Aircraft temperature and fuel flow systems instruments provide indications of whether the specific system is performing within its normal operating range.

Numerous temperature indications must be constantly monitored to ensure the safety of flight and proper operation of the aircraft engine. The most important indications include the engine oil, cylinder head, and exhaust systems of turbine engines.s.

Various types of thermometers, such as the bimetal and resistance types, collect and present this information. The bimetal thermometer is made of strips of two metals with different coefficients of expansion welded together and twisted in a spiral...

When the bimetal thermometer is heated, one of the strips expands more than the other and tries to straighten out the spiral. A pointer attached to the metal strip of the spiral moves across a dial to indicate changes in temperature...

Resistance change and voltage generation are two methods used in electrical temperature measurements. The main parts of resistance thermometers are the indicating instrument, the temperature-sensitive element (resistance bulb), and the connecting wires leading from the bulb...

The indicator dials of resistance thermometers are calibrated according to the range of temperature to be measured. The indicators are self-compensating, allowing for the changes in cockpit temperatures.s

Some resistance thermometers use a Wheatstone bridge circuit. A resistance bulb element from the monitored source is placed into one side of the circuit. The other three sides of the bridge are resistors mounted in the temperature indicator instrument...
When the temperature bulb senses a temperature of 0
C, its resistance is 100 ohms. The resistance of arms X, Y and Z
are also 100 ohms each. At this temperature, the Wheatstone
bridge is in balance. The sum of X and Y equals the sum of the bulb and Z.

When the resistance in a Wheatstone bridge is equal, the same amount of current flows in both sides of this parallel circuit and the voltage drop across side X equals the voltage drop across the bulb...

When the voltages are equal, the voltage measurement from A to B is zero, and the temperature indicator reads zero. As the temperature of the bulb changes, the resistance changes causing the bridge circuit to be unbalanced...

When the temperature of the bulb increases, its resistance increases. This unbalances the bridge circuit causing the needle to deflect to the right. As the bulb temperature decreases, the resistance decreases causing the needle to deflect to the left...
The ratiometer is a temperature indicator that uses two coils in a balanced circuit. There are two types of ratiometer circuits: moving-coil and moving-magnet.

In the moving-coil ratiometer, the coils turn between the poles of a permanent magnet with an attached indicator needle. In the moving-magnet ratiometer, a small permanent-magnet rotor with an attached needle turns between two stationary coils...

In the moving-coil ratiometer, when the temperature is low, the resistance in the bulb is low and more current flows through coil A and the bulb, than coil B and resistor R1. The resulting magnetic field pulls the needle to the low side...

When the temperature is high, the resistance in the bulb is high and more current flows through coil B and resistor R1, than coil A and the bulb. The resulting magnetic field deflects the needle to the high side of the indicator dial...

In the moving-magnet ratiometer, the two coils are stationary in the instrument, and the indicator needle fastens to the permanent-magnet rotor. The needle position is determined by how the permanent magnet aligns itself with the resultant flux of the two coils...

We trace the current flow in the circuit, by starting at ground. Current flows up through the resistance bulb, centering potentiometer R5 and R6, to point D. Current through the left leg of the bridge is from ground through R1 to point A...

Current then goes from point A through the lower part of the expansion and contraction potentiometer R2. It also goes from pin 2 of R2 through R4 to point D. The current from both legs combine and flow through R7 to the positive 28 volts...
The restoring coil L2, resistor R3, and the upper part of potentiometer R2 forms a parallel path for current flow from point A to pin 2 of R2. Deflection coil L1 connects between points A and B...

Any difference in potential between points A and B will cause current to flow through L1. Temperature changes sensed by the bulb cause a change in voltage at point B and causes a resultant current flow through the deflection coil L1...

As the temperature changes, the resistance of the bulb changes, causing current to flow in the coils L1 and L2 creating resultant lines of flux that cause the permanent-magnet with its attached needle to move left or right...

Thermocouple temperature indicators display the air temperatures in the heater duct of anti-icing systems, the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) of jet engines and cylinder head temperature (CHT) in reciprocating engines...
A thermocouple is a junction or connection of two unlike metals. Strips of iron and Constantan (copper/nickel alloy) or Chromel and Alumel are normally used in thermocouple junctions.

As one junction becomes hotter than the other, an electromotive force is produced in the circuit. By including galvanometers in the circuit, this electromotive force can be measured. By calibrating the galvanometers dial, in degrees of temperature, it becomes a thermometer...

The galvanometers in the indicator comprise the cold junction, while the hot junction of a thermocouple varies in shape, depending on its application. The common types of thermocouples are the gasket, bayonet and the screw-in...

Cylinder head temperature (CHT) is normally measured by a gasket thermocouple. Rings of two dissimilar metals are pressed together, forming a spark plug gasket. The gasket is called the hot or measuring junction..

A voltage proportional to the temperature difference between the junctions causes current to flow through the indicator. The indicator is a current measuring instrument that is calibrated in degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit...

Thermocouple leads are critical in makeup and length because the galvanometers are calibrated for a specific set of leads in the circuits. Crossed leads would cause the indicator needle to move off scale to the left...

High temperatures are measured on reciprocating and turbine engines using thermocouples made of Chromel and Alumel wires. On reciprocating engines, the thermocouple is mounted in the exhaust pipe within about six inches of the cylinder...

The exhaust gas temperature (EGT) indicating systems provide a visual temperature indication in the cockpit of the engine exhaust gases. Multi-engine aircraft contain two separate but identical EGT indicating systems, one for each engine...

Exhaust gas temperature (EGT) systems on turbine engines usually have 12 dual thermocouples arranged around the tail cone to sample the average EGT. Each instrument is a hermetically sealed unit with a single plug receptacle...
C. Internally, the indicator contains a simulated thermocouple cold junction with compensating resistors, a reference voltage source, and a DC-to-AC modulator.

The thermocouples convert engine exhaust gas temperature into millivolts. The voltage is amplified and drives a small servomotor. The motor, in turn, drives the indicator pointer to display the exhaust gas temperature...

Turbine inlet temperature (TIT) is the most critical temperature in a turbine engine. However, TIT is difficult to measure due to the high temperatures and high velocity of gases passing through the first stage of the turbine...
Turbine inlet temperature (TIT) indicator systems provide a visual indication of temperatures entering the turbine. Monitoring TIT while starting an engine can prevent a "HOT START".

All parts of the engine temperature measurement system are made of Chromel and Alumel material, including welds. Special wiring and wire identification are in the aircraft from the thermocouple harness terminal block to the indicator...

Plugs in the thermocouple circuits are also of a special type and can't be altered. The thermocouple harness mounts on the turbine unit aft of the thermocouple. The harness includes separate leads for each of the 18 thermocouples....

Electrical signals from the 18 dual-junction thermocouples are averaged within the harness. Since the average voltage of the thermocouples represents the TIT, a special wiring harness is used to prevent signal interference from other sources...

The TIT indicator contains a bridge circuit with cold junction compensation, a two-phase motor to drive the pointer, and a feedback potentiometer. A Zener voltage reference circuit, a chopper circuit, an amplifier, power supply, a power-off flag, and an over-temp warning light are also included...
The indicator scale is calibrated from 0
C in 2-degree increments. The bridge circuit output is amplified and fed to the variable field of the two-phase motor...

The two-phase motor in the TIT system is similar to the moving-magnet ratiometer. The flux from the variable field positions the magnetic rotor with the attached main pointer to indicate the turbine inlet temperature...

Fuel flow indicating systems provide a continuous indication of the rate of fuel delivery to the engine. The rate of flow is in pounds or gallons per hour. Some fuel system indicators also show the amount of fuel remaining in the tanks...

A typical fuel flowmeter consists of a transmitter and an indicator. The measurements are transmitted electrically to the panel-mounted indicator. Some fuel flowmeter systems are similar to the basic Autosyn (Synchro) systems...

The rotor shaft of the synchro transmitter connects to a bar magnet. A ring magnet is attached to the vane shaft and moves when the vane shaft moves. The transmitter-mounting frame forms a liquid-tight seal between the magnets...
The bar magnet and ring magnet move in unison because the two magnets are magnetically coupled. The south pole of the ring magnet is opposite the north pole of the bar magnet.
As fuel flows, the vane shaft with its attached ring magnet moves, magnetically moving the bar magnet. This action results in corresponding movement of the synchro rotor.

Therefore, the angular displacement of the vane in relation to the fuel chamber housing determines the synchro rotor movement with respect to the stator windings. The stator windings of the synchro transmitter are attached to the electrical connector...

A wire harness connects the output of the synchro transmitter to the fuel flow indicator on the instrument panel in the cockpit. The remote-indicating instrument consists of a synchro receiver, a step-up gear train, a magnetic drag cup, and a calibrated spring...

When fuel flows through the fuel flow transmitter, an electrical signal goes to the indicator receiver. This signal drives the synchro rotor with its attached pointer to the proper position and indicates the rate of fuel flow...
Computerized fuel systems use a small turbine rotor transducer mounted in the fuel line between the flow divider and the fuel injection nozzles.
Fuel flowing to the cylinders must pass through the turbine, which spins at a speed proportional to the rate of fuel flow.

As the turbine spins, it breaks a beam of light between a phototransistor and a light-emitting diode. The interrupted beam of light is converted into pulses of electricity, which are processed by a computer and displayed on the fuel flow indicator...

The fuel flowmeter most accurately indicates fuel consumption in reciprocating aircraft engines because it can be cross-checked with the electronic fuel quantity indicator.
The fuel flowmeter used with a continuous-fuel injection system installed on an aircraft horizontally opposed reciprocating engine measures the pressure drop across the fuel injector nozzles...

The pressure drop across the injector nozzles is a function of the volume of fuel flowing through them. If one of the injector nozzles were clogged, the pressure drop would increase indicating a false increase in fuel flow...

Aircraft instrument shape and size will vary with the type of aircraft and the manufacturer.

Instruments that have range markings on the glass rather than on the dial, must have a white slip mark to show if the glass has slipped in the case. The white slip mark is painted across the bezel onto the glass at the bottom of the instrument...

If the glass in an instrument slips, the range markings on the glass will be out of alignment with the numbers on the dial and the slip mark will be broken warning the pilot the instrument is no longer aligned...

The technician installing aircraft instruments in an instrument panel is responsible to ensure the instruments are secure in their mounting and that all attached hoses and wires are in good condition and do not interfere with any of the flight controls...

Most electrical instruments are mounted in steel or iron cases to prevent interference from nearby magnetic fields. Lines of magnetic flux do not flow through steel or iron, and are entrapped in these types of cases...

Remember, aircraft instruments can only be repaired or altered by the manufacturer or an FAA certified repair station approved for that particular instrument. Replacing range marks, tightening loose screws, tightening leaking B nuts in the plumbing and touching up chipped case paint are not considered to be repairs or alterations.....

In electronics, any component with resistance will heat up as current flows through it, due to the I R effects. In the case of heat generators, this effect is a desired result.

All resistive components have a property called Thermal Resistance ( R), which equates electrical watts to the temperature within the core of the device (or at the P-N junction of a solid-state component).

The Thermal Resistance rating for any component, describes how hot the component will become for each watt of electrical power that is applied to it, as indicated by the junction temperature dissipation equation: T = T + ( R x P )

The majority of temperature sensor outputs must be raised to useful analog levels for aircraft applications. Often, these analog signals are converted to digital signals for glass cockpit displays.

Thermocouple sensors are connected to temperature instruments by a wiring harness of specific length and wire type. To reduce the effects of Electromagnetic interference (EMI) in the harness, the Differential Amplifier is employed...

Notice that the differential amplifier is used to boost the signal from the thermocouple. Noise generated on the wiring harness is canceled due to the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) features of the amplifier...

Notice that two sensors are used in a Wheatstone bridge differential measurement device. The reference sensor is in one leg while the remote sensor is in the other. In this case, V is proportional to the difference in temperature between the sensors.

IC temperature transducers are commonly used in temperature measurement and control systems. The IC transducer produces an output current proportional to absolute (Kelvin) temperature and is fed into a temperature detector circuit to produce a DC voltage output...

The detector circuit uses a precise voltage to establish reference and stability for the DC voltage output. A 2.5 VDC regulated reference voltage from (U1) is sent to the ZERO potentiometer (R8), which compensates for circuit variations...
A dual voltage compensator (U3) and a D-Type flip-flop (U4) are used for Fan Control. One comparator (U3B) turns the fan ON while the second comparator (U3A) turns the fan OFF.

Two variable resistors R13 (OFF) and R14 (ON) are used to select the voltage that is translated into temperature to control the operation of the fan. When the transducer reaches a set temperature the fan will turn on...
The outputs of the comparators (Pin 1 of U3A and Pin 7 of U3B) are tied to the SET (Preset) and RESET (Clear) inputs of flip-flop U4A.

When U4A is SET (Q = HIGH) and switch S1 is in the manual position, Q1 turns ON, placing a LOW on DS2 (Fan On indicator) and M1 (Fan). With a LOW applied to the indicator and fan, both of them become active..

When U4A is RESET (Q = LOW) and switch S1 is in the manual position, Q1 turns OFF, placing a HIGH on DS2 (Fan On indicator) and M1 (fan). With a HIGH applied, both the indicator and the fan turn OFF...
